so I just blasted through this in a single sitting, and I have thoughts:

+ looks great, runs smoothly.
~ I am indifferent regarding the music. it's pretty forgettable, but it's not bad by any stretch otherwise.
+ the sound effects are nice, on the other hand.
+ the story has some pretty great twists and turns that are really unique.
+ the ending I got was incredibly satisfying, and I appreciate being allowed to side with either Thought or The Nation (I don't think that's a spoiler, this wouldn't be a very good story-driven, "choices matter" game if it didn't have multiple endings). for those who have played the game, I sided with Thought because not only do I agree with them, but also because I found them to be written in a nuanced way, that they were in the right as far as the narrative framing is concerned, and I thought that it was more interesting to try and cover for them, rather than obeying the fascists calling the shots. if you sided with The Nation for whatever reason, it's definitely worth trying Thought's ending, because it's morbidly hilarious what the final nail in the coffin you use is.
- without spoiling the ending, I have a few narrative problems which are just... not great to see? for starters, two members of Thought are giving their options for what they think you should do, but then they refer to the wrong one as their plan (ex. you can do my plan of going to the store, or the other one of staying home--but they're mixed up). they also seem to immediately learn complex concepts you had to be taught in the tutorial, like, immediately. one of them is tech savvy enough for me to buy it, but the other one isn't and they're the one who name-drops this hyper-specific jargon they shouldn't know. while this does not ruin my enjoyment of this story (hence my recommendation), it feels like there was a bit of a rush, where the ending goes.

overall, pretty damn intriguing, and it's not like a lot of media as of late which invokes George Orwell's legacy without truly understanding who he was as a person. that's enough for me to give it some level of praise.

Overall: I liked this game. I found this to be a thought-provoking experience, one that I really was dedicated to the characters and interested in the story.

The story revolves around an attack on a local landmark, to which you only have one lead: a woman who was arrested in connection to a riot in the same place. You dig around as a member of ORWELL, which is a very invasive project designed to gather any and all information on whoever their higher-ups authorize them to. As you gather more information, you get authorization to investigate more people tied to the first. It becomes interesting, and twists and turns along the way manage to catch you off guard.

The style of game-play is similar to how one would read a book to fill out a homework assignment, made easier by highlighting the important bits. I fell into that sort of thought process, and then the game became interesting. Usually, things are marked in blue, but a second marking, a yellow highlight, means there is conflicting information.

It went from a read and extract to a branching story - one that you could influence based on what you chose. In my first play-through, I tried to get the truth, or what I thought could be the truth, but what I had selected painted a bleak view of the suspects. I realize now that what I had chosen influenced how characters were perceived, which was a very nice touch. 

I recommend this game, especially for people who are into mystery and observation sims (is that a genre? This game is about government spying, so if you're into that, that's what I mean).

Very interesting game about government surveilance. The gameplay mechanic is simply to read text, find differently colored sections and decide if you will add that information to a persons profile. The catch is that sometimes the info could be interpreted in a negative light when it was just a joke between friends. So there is a lot of responsibility on the shoulders of the person doing the data entry. Sometimes it's a matter of life and death and you don't always have all the facts, so you're forced to take a chance based on your intuition about who someone is. There is a political message in the game, but it's subtle and it lets you draw your own conclusions about how things are. The game doesn't tell you what to think.

I've never actually made a review for a game before, but as I got the last achievement(which I did in only - I think - three games I own) and finished the game for like the fourth time, I think a positive review is mandatory. 

God, I love this game.

I'm a fan of these "political simulators" as I've seen these kinds of games adressed as, those where the player works for the government/media or some other important institution and makes decisions that later change the lives of the characters around them in various ways.

In this game, you play as an investigator for a nation-wide surveillance program, in which you have to collect information on potentially dangerous(according to your superiors at least) people and put them into a system, based on which the people above you then act(I suppose it's kind of a bad description, but whatever), and it's probably the best game of it's kind for me, though people might be inclined to disagree.

Orwell required some logical thinking, but not to a degree it was difficult, which I liked - I had to think about it, but I wouldn't get lost in it. I liked the characters, they were fun, none of them was obnoxious to me(some find the advisor - the character of your coworker, that at first guides you through the game and to who you forward your chosen information you find - very obnoxious, but for me, he was the best character, honestly), and I liked seeing the details, or bigger things change based on the choices I made in various routes.

I'd say the game has some replay value - if just to see the three more endings you didn't get on the first try, or to change  the fates of some characters who's lives you directly influenced through your actions.

It's a text based game, so I wouldn't recommend it to people who don't like to read much while playing games, but I think that's obvious from the pictures, videos, maybe even premise...

There's one thing I could think of critiquing right now, which is that when you're listening to people's phone calls or reading their texts in the game, at least to me it's lengthy even if you have the speed of those things set to the highest, mainly during replays.

I'm not sure if I'd buy it for ten euros though - I bought this game on sale, but then again, I bought almost all the games I own on Steam during a sale. If I think about it... I'd probably buy it for the full price now, knowing just how much I liked it, but if you aren't completely sure you're going to love it, I would probably wait for a sale. But maybe I just don't like spending too much money on Steam, since the price isn't even THAT high if I look at it transcribed to my country's currency.

Overall, I can say that I enjoyed Orwell very much, it's one of my most favorite games of all time, even if it might not be one of the objectively best games I played, it is one of the best for me, and I'd recommend it to anyone who would ask.

I really wanted to like this game more.
Initially I was very intrigued, however the longer I played the more everything started to fall apart.
First off - this needs voice acting.
I don't think every line in the game needs voice acting, but at least the phone calls and the advisers should've been voiced.
Secondly - add more red herrings/alternative plot lines that a player can trip on.
This game initially seemed very vast and branched out to me, yet as I played it through and then replayed a couple more times for the achievements I realised that it is still very linear and there's not much you can do that will have a very big effect on your playthrough.
Third - there were a few plot lines in the game that were just never explained or touched on again. I think the game could've been more fleshed out if these plotlines were explored more.
Fourth - not being able to change datachunks. I understand that the whole plot is built on the idea that you cannot keep changing data, but it just felt like an artificial boundary for seemingly no reason.
Lastly - I couldn't help but feel like some of the writing for the characters was just off (it's hard to put into words but something just didn't feel right about the way the interactions went).

Overall the game was ok, but its just not something I would recommend to someone else.
